newsitem.title: UK: British Telecom admits to MCI culture gap.
newsitem.headline: British Telecom admits to MCI culture gap.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc admitted Thursday to not sharing the same corporate culture as merger partner MCI Communications Corp., America's second largest long-distance telephone company.

But, after reporting robust third-quarter profits, helped by "healthy" demand for its products and services, British Telecommunications' Chief Executive Sir Peter Bonfield, told reporters, "We are open-minded that these things (mergers) have their pitfalls on culture."
Commentators have dubbed British Telecom "staid" and MCI "spunky."

But Bonfield said MCI staff members he had met so far had been "amazingly enthusiastic" about the two companies' planned $20 billion merger, which British Telecom expects European and American regulators to approve by this fall.

British Telecom reported a rise in third-quarter pretax profits to 909 million pounds ($1.45 billion) from 829 million pounds ($1.36 billion) in the previous year's quarter after a 39-million-pound ($64 million) charge for layoffs. The figure was toward the upper end of analysts' expectations.

British Telecom announced last October that it planned to buy the 80 percent of Washington-based MCI it did not already own. The new company, called Concert Plc, aims to sell its services to multinational companies at all levels and be represented in all the world's key nations.
British Telecom also hopes to become the second telecommunications power in Continental Europe as key markets are eased open to competition in 1998 and is itching to get into lucrative Asian markets.
British Telecom has one of the most comprehensive network partnerships across Europe, having set up joint ventures in about eight Continental European markets worth more than $140 billion.

In a move to boost its German venture, British Telecom announced that Norway's Telenor had agreed in principle to take a 10 percent stake in VIAG InterKom, the alliance British Telecom has set up with German engineering conglomerate VIAG AG.

Telenor brings with it vital expertise from operating in one of the world's most saturated markets for mobile telephones. Having won a mobile and fixed-line license in Germany, British Telecom said VIAG InterKom would be the first major telecommunications company to exploit the convergence between the two services.
In December, British Telecom beat archrivals Deutsche Telekom and France Telecom by clinching a deal with TeleDanmark in Switzerland's second telecommunications network, Newtelco.
